content: Anemia is the most prevalent blood disorder. The term anemia originates from the Greek word an-haîma, meaning without blood. It is characterized by a deficiency in red blood cells (RBCs) and/or hemoglobin, which leads to a reduced capacity of the blood to transport oxygen to tissues, resulting in tissue hypoxia. Since oxygen is essential for the survival of all human cells, varying degrees of anemia can lead to a wide range of clinical consequences. Hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in RBCs, is crucial for ensuring adequate oxygenation of tissues and organs. Anemia can be classified into three main categories based on its underlying cause: excessive blood loss (either acute, such as hemorrhage, or chronic, such as low-volume loss), excessive destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis), or insufficient production of red blood cells (ineffective hematopoiesis). Anemia is defined as a hemoglobin concentration of less than 12 g/dL in women and less than 13 g/dL in men, or a hematocrit of less than 36% in women and less than 40% in men. Anemia can be categorized in several ways, including the morphology of RBCs, the underlying etiologic mechanisms, and the clinical spectrum. Two major approaches to classification are the kinetic approach, which evaluates production, destruction, and loss, and the morphologic approach, which groups anemia based on RBC size. The morphologic approach often begins with the mean corpuscular volume (MCV), a readily available and cost-effective laboratory test. However, focusing on production early in the diagnostic process may help clinicians identify cases with multiple coexisting causes of anemia more quickly. Erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone produced in the kidneys, is the primary stimulant for RBC production in response to anemia. Tissue hypoxia triggers the release of EPO, which stimulates erythroid progenitor cells to proliferate. EPO levels are inversely related to hemoglobin levels; in healthy individuals, low hemoglobin levels are associated with high EPO levels. However, in patients with chronic kidney disease or anemia of chronic diseases, the EPO response may be blunted compared to individuals without these comorbidities. The causes of anemia can be divided based on the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) into microcytic, macrocytic, and normocytic anemia. Common causes of microcytic anemia include iron deficiency, thalassemia, anemia of chronic disease, and sideroblastic anemia (which may be congenital or caused by lead, alcohol, or drugs). Macrocytic anemia is often caused by alcohol abuse, folic acid deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, myelodysplastic disorders, acute myeloid leukemias, drug-induced anemia (e.g., hydroxyurea, AZT, chemotherapeutic agents), reticulocytosis, and liver disease. Normocytic anemia is commonly caused by acute blood loss, anemia of chronic disease, bone marrow suppression, chronic renal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and hyperthyroidism. Anemia often goes undetected in many individuals, as its symptoms can be vague. The clinical presentation of anemia varies depending on the rapidity of onset, hematocrit levels, and the patient’s overall health, including factors such as age, sex, pregnancy, cardiac conditions, and other comorbidities. A hematocrit level between 30-35% typically produces no symptoms, while a drop to 15-20% may result in severe symptoms such as shortness of breath and syncope. Most patients experience symptoms when hemoglobin levels fall to approximately 7 g/dL. The physical examination findings in anemia are often nonspecific and similar across different types of anemia. The presentation depends on the acuity of onset, hematocrit levels, and the patient’s general health rather than solely on the underlying cause of anemia. A complete blood count (CBC) is the initial diagnostic test for anemia. The CBC measures various parameters, including the mean corpuscular volume (MCV), red blood cell count, hemoglobin levels, and red blood cell distribution width (RDW). These values allow for the calculation of other indices, such as hematocrit, mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC). Primary prevention of iron deficiency anemia involves consuming iron-rich foods. Certain foods, however, can interfere with iron absorption in the gastrointestinal tract and should be avoided by individuals with established iron deficiency. These include tea, coffee, wheat bran, rhubarb, chocolate, chewing gum, red wine, and dairy products.
